name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q01 - Taxonomic classification systems and their scientific bases

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Artificial classification system I. Based on natural affinities and internal features like ultrastructure and anatomy
B. Natural classification system II. Based on chemical constituents of the plant to resolve confusions
C. Cytotaxonomy III. Based on cytological information like chromosome number, structure, and behaviour
D. Chemotaxonomy IV. Based on gross superficial vegetative characters or androecium structure

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the artificial classification system.
The earliest systems of classification, such as the one proposed by Linnaeus, were artificial. They relied on gross superficial morphological characters, vegetative characters, or sexual characteristics such as the androecium structure.

Step 2: Understand the natural classification system.
Natural classification systems, such as the one developed by George Bentham and Joseph Dalton Hooker for flowering plants, were based on natural affinities among organisms. These systems evaluated not only external morphology but also internal features such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology, and phytochemistry.

Step 3: Understand cytotaxonomy.
Cytotaxonomy is a branch of taxonomy that resolves classification problems using cytological information, specifically chromosome number, chromosome structure, and chromosome behaviour during division.

Step 4: Understand chemotaxonomy.
Chemotaxonomy is utilized by taxonomists to resolve ambiguities and confusions in classification by evaluating the chemical constituents and phytochemical profile of plants.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Connecting each system to its foundational principle reveals: - Artificial classification system corresponds to being based on gross superficial vegetative characters or androecium structure. - Natural classification system corresponds to being based on natural affinities and internal features like ultrastructure and anatomy. - Cytotaxonomy corresponds to being based on cytological information like chromosome number, structure, and behaviour. - Chemotaxonomy corresponds to being based on chemical constituents of the plant to resolve confusions.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q02 - Storage food products across different algal classes

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Chlorophyceae I. Floridean starch
B. Phaeophyceae II. Mannitol and laminarin
C. Rhodophyceae III. Starch
D. Pyrenoids IV. Protein besides starch

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify storage food in Chlorophyceae.
Members of Chlorophyceae (green algae) primarily store food in the form of starch. Most members possess specialized storage bodies called pyrenoids located within the chloroplasts.

Step 2: Identify storage food in Phaeophyceae.
Members of Phaeophyceae (brown algae) store reserve food as complex carbohydrates, characteristically in the forms of laminarin or mannitol.

Step 3: Identify storage food in Rhodophyceae.
Members of Rhodophyceae (red algae) store food as floridean starch, whose molecular structure is highly similar to amylopectin and glycogen.

Step 4: Identify the chemical nature of pyrenoids.
Pyrenoids are distinct sub-cellular storage bodies located in the chloroplasts of green algae; biochemically, they contain protein surrounded by a starch sheath (protein besides starch).

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Matching each class and cellular structure with its stored reserve material yields: - Chlorophyceae corresponds to starch. - Phaeophyceae corresponds to mannitol and laminarin. - Rhodophyceae corresponds to floridean starch. - Pyrenoids correspond to containing protein besides starch.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q03 - Gamete motility and types of sexual reproduction

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Isogamous with flagellated gametes I. Spirogyra
B. Isogamous with non-flagellated gametes II. Ulothrix
C. Anisogamous reproduction III. Volvox
D. Oogamous reproduction IV. Eudorina

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze flagellated isogamous reproduction.
In isogamous reproduction, fusing gametes are morphologically similar in size. When these fusing gametes are flagellated and motile, as observed in Ulothrix, reproduction is isogamous with flagellated gametes.

Step 2: Analyze non-flagellated isogamous reproduction.
When fusing gametes are similar in size but non-flagellated (non-motile), as seen in the filamentous green alga Spirogyra, the condition is isogamous with non-motile gametes.

Step 3: Analyze anisogamous reproduction.
Anisogamy involves the fusion of two gametes that are dissimilar in size. Species of Eudorina characteristically exhibit anisogamous sexual reproduction.

Step 4: Analyze oogamous reproduction.
Oogamy represents the fusion between one large, static, non-motile female gamete and a smaller, motile male gamete. Classic textbook examples include colonial forms such as Volvox and brown algae such as Fucus.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Aligning each mode of sexual reproduction with its textbook representative species produces: - Isogamous with flagellated gametes corresponds to Ulothrix. - Isogamous with non-flagellated gametes corresponds to Spirogyra. - Anisogamous reproduction corresponds to Eudorina. - Oogamous reproduction corresponds to Volvox.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q04 - Commercial products derived from specific algal species

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Algin I. Gelidium and Gracilaria
B. Carrageen II. Brown algae
C. Agar III. Chlorella
D. Food supplement for space travellers IV. Red algae

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the source of algin.
Certain marine brown algae produce substantial quantities of hydrocolloids (water-holding substances), of which algin is commercially extracted from brown algae.

Step 2: Identify the source of carrageen.
Carrageen is another commercially utilized hydrocolloid that is specifically harvested and purified from marine red algae.

Step 3: Identify the source of agar.
Agar is an important commercial product used to culture microorganisms and in the food industry to prepare ice-creams and jellies; it is extracted from the red algal genera Gelidium and Gracilaria.

Step 4: Identify the unicellular food supplement for space travellers.
Chlorella is a unicellular green alga rich in proteins that serves as an essential nutritional food supplement, utilized even by astronauts during space travel.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Synthesizing the product-to-source relationships gives: - Algin corresponds to brown algae. - Carrageen corresponds to red algae. - Agar corresponds to Gelidium and Gracilaria. - Food supplement for space travellers corresponds to Chlorella.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q05 - Cell wall and flagellar features of algae

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Chlorophyceae flagella I. 2, unequal, laterally attached
B. Phaeophyceae flagella II. Completely absent in spores and gametes
C. Rhodophyceae flagella III. 2–8, equal, apically attached
D. Phaeophyceae cell wall IV. Cellulosic wall covered on outside by a gelatinous coating of algin

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine flagellar features of green algae (Chlorophyceae).
Motile stages (zoospores and gametes) in Chlorophyceae possess 2 to 8 flagella that are identical in length (equal) and inserted at the anterior tip (apical).

Step 2: Determine flagellar features of brown algae (Phaeophyceae).
Zoospores and gametes in Phaeophyceae are pyriform (pear-shaped) and bear 2 flagella that are unequal in length and laterally attached.

Step 3: Determine flagellar features of red algae (Rhodophyceae).
Rhodophyceae reproduce asexually by non-motile spores and sexually by non-motile gametes; flagella are completely absent throughout their entire life cycle.

Step 4: Determine cell wall characteristics of Phaeophyceae.
Vegetative cells of brown algae have a cellulosic inner wall typically coated externally with a gelatinous, protective colloidal substance called algin.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Pairing each anatomical diagnostic feature correctly gives: - Chlorophyceae flagella corresponds to 2–8, equal, apically attached. - Phaeophyceae flagella corresponds to 2, unequal, laterally attached. - Rhodophyceae flagella corresponds to completely absent in spores and gametes. - Phaeophyceae cell wall corresponds to cellulosic wall covered on outside by a gelatinous coating of algin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q06 - Morphological and juvenile structures in bryophyte biology

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Gemmae I. Creeping, green, branched, and frequently filamentous juvenile stage
B. Protonema II. Green, multicellular, asexual buds developed in receptacles on the thallus
C. Peat III. Fuel and trans-shipment packing material obtained from Sphagnum
D. Leafy stage of moss IV. Upright, slender axis bearing spirally arranged leaves and sex organs

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define gemmae.
In liverworts such as Marchantia, asexual reproduction occurs through gemmae, which are green, multicellular, asexual buds produced inside specialized cups called gemma cups on the dorsal thallus.

Step 2: Define protonema.
In mosses, the spore directly germinates into the primary protonema stage, which is characterized as a creeping, green, branched, and frequently filamentous juvenile gametophytic phase.

Step 3: Define peat.
Species of the moss Sphagnum accumulate to form peat, historically used as fuel and commercially as packing material for the trans-shipment of living specimens owing to its high water-retention capacity.

Step 4: Define the leafy stage of a moss.
The second developmental gametophytic stage of a moss develops from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud; it consists of an upright, slender axis bearing spirally arranged leaves and multicellular branched rhizoids, and it bears the sex organs.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Assigning each structure to its biological description gives: - Gemmae corresponds to green, multicellular, asexual buds developed in receptacles on the thallus. - Protonema corresponds to creeping, green, branched, and frequently filamentous juvenile stage. - Peat corresponds to fuel and trans-shipment packing material obtained from Sphagnum. - Leafy stage of moss corresponds to upright, slender axis bearing spirally arranged leaves and sex organs.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q07 - Classes of pteridophytes and their representative genera

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Psilopsida I. Equisetum
B. Lycopsida II. Selaginella and Lycopodium
C. Sphenopsida III. Dryopteris, Pteris, and Adiantum
D. Pteropsida IV. Psilotum

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classify Psilopsida.
The class Psilopsida includes primitive, rootless vascular plants with photosynthetic axes; its textbook representative genus is Psilotum.

Step 2: Classify Lycopsida.
The class Lycopsida (club mosses and spike mosses) is characterized by microphyllous leaves and includes the genera Selaginella and Lycopodium.

Step 3: Classify Sphenopsida.
The class Sphenopsida (horsetails) is distinguished by articulated stems with nodes, internodes, and whorled branches; its sole living representative is Equisetum.

Step 4: Classify Pteropsida.
The class Pteropsida includes true ferns possessing macrophyllous leaves (fronds); representative genera cited are Dryopteris, Pteris, and Adiantum.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Matching each pteridophyte class to its corresponding genera gives: - Psilopsida corresponds to Psilotum. - Lycopsida corresponds to Selaginella and Lycopodium. - Sphenopsida corresponds to Equisetum. - Pteropsida corresponds to Dryopteris, Pteris, and Adiantum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q08 - Specialized root and leaf adaptations in gymnosperms

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Coralloid roots I. Symbiotic fungal association with roots in Pinus
B. Mycorrhiza II. Specialized apogeotropic roots associated with \(N_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria in Cycas
C. Sunken stomata and thick cuticle III. Xerophytic adaptations in conifers to minimize water loss
D. Unbranched stem with persistent pinnate leaves IV. Distinct vegetative shoot morphology in Cycas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand coralloid roots.
In Cycas, small, specialized roots called coralloid roots grow near the surface and maintain a symbiotic relationship with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria (such as Anabaena or Nostoc).

Step 2: Understand mycorrhizal roots.
In Pinus, roots establish an obligate symbiotic association with fungal hyphae known as mycorrhiza, which assists the plant in mineral and water absorption.

Step 3: Understand conifer leaf xerophytic features.
In conifers, leaves are needle-like to reduce overall surface area. In addition, their thick cuticle and sunken stomata strongly restrict transpiration, enabling them to withstand extremes of wind, temperature, and aridity.

Step 4: Understand stem and leaf morphology in cycads.
While conifers such as Pinus and Cedrus possess branched stems, Cycas is distinguished by having an unbranched columnar stem crowned with large pinnately compound leaves that persist for several years.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Correlating each botanical feature with its respective role and taxon gives: - Coralloid roots corresponds to specialized apogeotropic roots associated with \(N_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria in Cycas. - Mycorrhiza corresponds to symbiotic fungal association with roots in Pinus. - Sunken stomata and thick cuticle corresponds to xerophytic adaptations in conifers to minimize water loss. - Unbranched stem with persistent pinnate leaves corresponds to distinct vegetative shoot morphology in Cycas.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q09 - Key reproductive structures in gymnosperm life cycle

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Pollen grain I. Differentiated from one cell of the nucellus and divides meiotically
B. Megaspore mother cell II. Highly reduced male gametophyte confined to a limited number of cells
C. Multicellular female gametophyte III. Retained within megasporangium and bears two or more archegonia
D. Gymnosperm ovule IV. Integumented megasporangium borne exposed on megasporophylls

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the nature of gymnosperm pollen grain.
In gymnosperms, microspores develop within microsporangia into a highly reduced male gametophyte confined to only a limited number of cells, commonly designated as the pollen grain.

Step 2: Understand the origin of the megaspore mother cell.
Within the ovule, one central cell of the parenchymatous nucellus differentiates into the megaspore mother cell, which undergoes meiosis to form four haploid megaspores.

Step 3: Understand the multicellular female gametophyte (endosperm).
One functional megaspore develops into a multicellular female gametophyte that remains permanently enclosed inside the megasporangium and bears two or more archegonia.

Step 4: Understand the gymnosperm ovule.
The gymnosperm ovule is an integumented nucellus (megasporangium) that is not enclosed by an ovary wall and remains completely exposed on megasporophylls before and after fertilisation.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Connecting each reproductive structure to its developmental and anatomical identity yields: - Pollen grain corresponds to highly reduced male gametophyte confined to a limited number of cells. - Megaspore mother cell corresponds to differentiated from one cell of the nucellus and divides meiotically. - Multicellular female gametophyte corresponds to retained within megasporangium and bears two or more archegonia. - Gymnosperm ovule corresponds to integumented megasporangium borne exposed on megasporophylls.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANT_KINGDOM_MATCH_LIST_Q10 - Evolutionary and life cycle milestones across plants

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I List II
A. Heterospory and female gametophyte retention I. Evolutionary precursor to the seed habit in Selaginella and Salvinia
B. Dominant sporophyte with free-living prothallus II. Sexual reproduction with non-motile gametes and post-fertilisation stages in Rhodophyceae
C. Sporophyte dependent on gametophyte III. Nutritional dependence of multicellular generation in Bryophytes
D. Oogamy with complex post-fertilisation developments IV. Characteristic life cycle alternation of generations in Pteridophytes

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand heterospory and the seed habit precursor.
In heterosporous pteridophytes such as Selaginella and Salvinia, megaspores develop into female gametophytes that are retained on the parent sporophytes. The zygote develops into an embryo within this retained female gametophyte, which represents a crucial evolutionary precursor to the seed habit.

Step 2: Understand the pteridophyte life cycle organisation.
In pteridophytes, the dominant independent plant body is a diploid vascular sporophyte, which alternates with a small, inconspicuous, photosynthetic, free-living haploid gametophyte termed the prothallus.

Step 3: Understand the bryophyte generational relationship.
In bryophytes, the dominant free-living generation is the haploid gametophyte. The diploid sporophyte is not free-living; it remains physically attached to and derives all its nourishment directly from the photosynthetic gametophyte.

Step 4: Understand reproduction in Rhodophyceae.
Red algae (Rhodophyceae) are characterized by non-motile spores and non-motile gametes. Sexual reproduction is advanced oogamy accompanied by elaborate and complex post-fertilisation developments.

Step 5: Conclude the matching pairs.
Connecting each life-cycle phenomenon to its evolutionary and taxonomic significance gives: - Heterospory and female gametophyte retention corresponds to evolutionary precursor to the seed habit in Selaginella and Salvinia. - Dominant sporophyte with free-living prothallus corresponds to characteristic life cycle alternation of generations in Pteridophytes. - Sporophyte dependent on gametophyte corresponds to nutritional dependence of multicellular generation in Bryophytes. - Oogamy with complex post-fertilisation developments corresponds to sexual reproduction with non-motile gametes and post-fertilisation stages in Rhodophyceae.
